name: Muscular System
tagline: The living ropes that move you, brace you, and breathe for you.
summary:
Muscle is the body's pulling tissue, and it is not confined to your arms and legs: smooth muscle sits in the walls of your blood vessels and gut, and cardiac muscle never stops in your heart. When people say the muscular system, they usually mean the 600-plus skeletal muscles that attach to bone and pull on it. They make up roughly 40 percent of an adult's body weight. More than bone, muscle gives a body its shape.

Skeletal muscle is built in layers. Bundles of fibers, each finer than a thread, are wrapped in connective tissue and gathered into a belly that tapers into tendons. A tendon anchors the muscle to bone across a joint, so when the fibers shorten by a fraction of their length, the bone swings through a wide arc. These muscles work in pairs: one bends a joint while its partner straightens it.

Two other muscle types keep you alive without a thought. Smooth muscle slowly squeezes blood vessels and pushes food through the intestine, while cardiac muscle contracts rhythmically in your heart. Together these tissues move you, warm you, and hold you together, and they respond to use. Load them with movement and they grow stronger; leave them idle and they waste away. That adaptability is the system's defining trait: muscle is tissue that rebuilds itself in response to use.

stats.label: of your body weight is muscle
your smallest muscle, in your ear

functions: Moves you by pulling on bones across joints
Pushes food through your gut and blood through your vessels
Shapes your body and guards your joints
Lets you breathe by changing the size of your chest

organs.name: Deltoid
organs.tagline: The triangular cap that lets you lift your arm out to the side.
organs.summary:
The deltoid is the triangular muscle that gives your shoulder its rounded cap. It has three parts that converge from the collarbone, the acromion, and the spine of the shoulder blade onto a rough patch on the outer upper arm called the deltoid tuberosity. Because the three parts pull from different angles, they can act almost like three muscles in one.

The middle part lifts your arm out to the side, the front part swings it forward, and the back part pulls it behind you. Lifting your arm overhead is a relay: a small muscle above the joint, the supraspinatus, starts the first few degrees, then the deltoid takes over. It also steadies the head of the arm bone in its shallow socket. Without a working deltoid, the shoulder would hang low and the arm would be hard to raise. It is the muscle you feel burning when you hold your arms out and make slow circles.

functions.title: Lifts the arm sideways
functions.detail: The middle fibers abduct the arm, carrying it from your side up toward shoulder height and beyond.

functions.title: Swings the arm forward and back
functions.detail: Front fibers flex the shoulder for reaching, while back fibers extend it for pushing and rowing.

functions.title: Steadies the shoulder joint
functions.detail: The muscle wraps the head of the humerus and helps keep it centered in its shallow socket.

functions.title: Carries loads at your side
functions.detail: Hang a heavy bag from your hand and the deltoid fires to keep the arm bone centered as the weight pulls down.

organs.location: It caps the shoulder joint, wrapping from the collarbone and shoulder blade down to the outer upper arm.
organs.size: Its fibers fan from collarbone to shoulder blade and thin into a flat tendon no wider than two fingers.
facts: The name comes from the Greek letter delta, because the muscle's outline looks like a triangle.
Many vaccines are injected into its thick middle part because the muscle is easy to reach.
Its three parts can fire independently, so one muscle can lift your arm forward, sideways, or backward.

conditions.name: Deltoid strain
conditions.description: Overstretching or tearing of the muscle fibers, often after heavy lifting or a sudden pull on the arm, causing pain and weakness when raising the arm.

conditions.name: Axillary nerve injury
conditions.description: The nerve that powers the deltoid can be stretched by a shoulder dislocation or a fracture, leaving the muscle weak and the shoulder rounded.

conditions.name: Subacromial bursitis
conditions.description: The fluid-filled sac beneath the deltoid can become inflamed, making it painful to lift the arm out to the side.

organs.name: Pectoralis Major
organs.tagline: The broad fan across your chest that pulls your arm inward.
organs.summary:
Your pectoralis major is the broad, fan-shaped muscle under the skin of your chest. It begins in several strips along the collarbone, the breastbone, and the upper ribs, then sweeps outward and gathers into a single tendon that attaches to the upper arm. As the fibers gather, they twist about 180 degrees, so the ones that start lowest on the chest end up highest on the arm.

Its main job is to pull the arm across the body and rotate it inward, the motion of a hug or a swimming stroke. The upper fibers also lift the arm forward, which is why a bench press works the chest so hard. Because the tendon crosses the front of the shoulder joint, the pectoralis major helps hold the arm bone in place. Push against a heavy door and you will feel the fan tighten across your chest.

functions.title: Pulls the arm across the chest
functions.detail: Adduction brings the arm inward, the motion of a hug, a push-up, or a swimming stroke.

functions.title: Rotates the arm inward
functions.detail: Medial rotation turns the forearm and hand toward the body, as when you reach across to scratch your back.

functions.title: Raises the arm forward
functions.detail: The clavicular fibers lift the arm in front of you, helping with overhead reaching and lifting.

functions.title: Helps you breathe hard
functions.detail: When you are out of breath, the pectoralis major can pull the ribs upward and assist the diaphragm.

organs.location: It spreads across the front of the chest, from the collarbone and breastbone to the upper arm.
organs.size: The fan spans from collarbone to lower ribs and narrows to a tendon about two fingers wide at the armpit.
facts: A smaller muscle, the pectoralis minor, hides beneath it and ties the shoulder blade to the ribs.
Some people are born without a pectoralis major on one side, a condition called Poland syndrome.
The collarbone and breastbone heads can act separately: one lifts the arm, the other pulls it across the chest.

conditions.name: Pectoralis major strain
conditions.description: A stretch or tear of the chest muscle, most often during heavy pushing or a sudden pull, causing pain near the armpit and weakness in the hug motion.

conditions.name: Pectoralis major tear
conditions.description: A complete rupture usually happens at the tendon near the arm bone, often during bench pressing, and can leave a visible dent in the chest.

conditions.name: Poland syndrome
conditions.description: A rare condition present at birth in which the pectoralis major is missing or underdeveloped on one side, sometimes with differences in the hand.

organs.name: Rectus Abdominis
organs.tagline: The strap of muscle that braces your trunk and curls you forward.
organs.summary:
Rectus abdominis is the long, flat strap of muscle that runs straight down the front of your belly. It starts at the pubic bone and climbs to the breastbone and the lower ribs, widening as it goes. Three or four bands of tough connective tissue cross it horizontally, dividing the muscle into the blocks people call a six-pack.

The muscle bends your trunk forward, the way you curl up from lying down, and it braces your spine when you lift something heavy. It also squeezes the abdominal contents, raising the pressure inside your belly when you cough, laugh, or push. Two sheets of fascia wrap it like a corset, and a seam of tissue called the linea alba separates the left and right halves. Every one of those blocks is part of the same muscle, not a separate one.

functions.title: Curls the trunk forward
functions.detail: It pulls your rib cage toward your pelvis, the motion of a curl-up or sitting up in bed.

functions.title: Braces the core
functions.detail: Contracting it stiffens the trunk so forces pass safely through the spine when you lift.

functions.title: Raises abdominal pressure
functions.detail: It squeezes the belly contents, raising pressure inside the abdomen during coughing, laughing, and pushing.

functions.title: Steadies the pelvis
functions.detail: It helps tilt and hold the pelvis while you walk, run, and kick.

organs.location: It runs vertically down the front of the abdomen, from the pubic bone to the breastbone.
organs.size: Each half is a flat strap about three fingers wide, wrapped in a sheath that is strongest near the midline.
facts: The six-pack is a single muscle crossed by bands of tendon; the blocks are not separate muscles.
Everyone has the bands; whether you can see them depends on body fat, not on doing more sit-ups.
It never touches your spine; it braces the trunk by linking your pelvis to your rib cage.

conditions.name: Diastasis recti
conditions.description: The gap between the two halves of the muscle widens, often after pregnancy, leaving a soft ridge down the middle of the belly.

conditions.name: Abdominal strain
conditions.description: A pulled abdominal muscle causes pain with curling, coughing, or laughing, and is common in sports that involve twisting.

conditions.name: Ventral hernia
conditions.description: A weakness in the abdominal wall lets a loop of intestine bulge through, appearing as a lump under the skin.

organs.name: Trapezius
organs.tagline: The kite-shaped muscle that shrugs, steadies, and braces your neck.
organs.summary:
The trapezius is a large, kite-shaped muscle that covers much of your upper back and neck. It starts along the base of the skull, the ligament at the back of the neck, and the bumps of the spine from the neck down to the middle of the back. From there its fibers fan out to the collarbone, the shoulder blade, and the ridge across the shoulder blade.

Its upper fibers lift your shoulder when you shrug, the middle fibers squeeze the shoulder blades together, and the lower fibers pull them down and help rotate them upward when you reach overhead. Working together, the three parts steady the shoulder blade so the arm can move with control. Its main nerve is a cranial nerve, the spinal accessory nerve, though small branches from the neck join in. A long day at a desk leaves it aching between your shoulder blades.

functions.title: Shrugs the shoulders
functions.detail: Upper fibers lift the shoulder blade, as when you carry a heavy backpack.

functions.title: Squeezes the shoulder blades
functions.detail: Middle fibers pull the scapulae toward the spine, helping you sit and stand taller.

functions.title: Rotates the shoulder blade upward
functions.detail: Lower fibers help turn the socket upward so the arm can reach overhead.

functions.title: Extends and tilts the neck
functions.detail: Working on one side, the upper fibers help tilt your head toward your shoulder and hold it against gravity.

organs.location: It lies just under the skin of the upper back and neck, spanning from the skull to the middle of the back.
organs.size: The two muscles together form a kite that spans from the base of your skull to the middle of your back, about the length of your forearm and hand.
facts: Its name comes from the trapezoid shape formed by the two muscles together.
Most muscles answer to spinal nerves; this one answers to a cranial nerve, the accessory nerve.
Its upper and lower fibers pull in opposite directions, yet together they rotate the shoulder blade upward when you reach overhead.

conditions.name: Trapezius strain
conditions.description: Stretched fibers in the upper back or neck cause aching and stiffness, often after prolonged desk work or a sudden lift.

conditions.name: Myofascial pain
conditions.description: Tight bands in the muscle, called trigger points, can refer pain up the neck and into the head.

conditions.name: Spinal accessory nerve injury
conditions.description: Damage to the nerve that drives the trapezius weakens the shrug and can make the shoulder blade drift outward.

organs.name: Biceps Brachii
organs.tagline: The two-headed muscle that bends your elbow and turns your palm up.
organs.summary:
The biceps brachii is the muscle that pops up on the front of your upper arm when you make a fist and bend your elbow. It has two heads: a long head that starts on the rim of the shoulder socket and a short head that starts on a bony hook at the front of the shoulder blade. Both bellies merge into one tendon that grips the radius, the bone on the thumb side of your forearm.

The biceps bends your elbow, but its specialty is turning your palm to face upward, a motion called supination. That is why it feels strongest when you lift a heavy box with your palms up. It also helps lift your arm at the shoulder. Because its long tendon runs through the shoulder joint, it can be irritated by repeated overhead work. Flex your arm now and you are watching two heads of one muscle work as a team.

functions.title: Bends the elbow
functions.detail: It is a powerful flexor of the elbow, especially when your palm faces up.

functions.title: Turns the palm upward
functions.detail: Supination is its specialty; the biceps is the strongest supinator of the forearm.

functions.title: Lifts the arm
functions.detail: It assists shoulder flexion, helping you bring your hand toward your face.

functions.title: Steadies the shoulder
functions.detail: The long head tendon passes through the joint and helps stabilize the head of the arm bone.

organs.location: It sits on the front of the upper arm, between the shoulder and the elbow.
organs.size: Its belly runs about a hand's length down the front of the arm and tapers into tendons at both ends.
facts: Biceps means two heads, and both heads start at the shoulder but from different points.
It is the strongest supinator of the forearm, which is why a stubborn jar lid yields to a palm-up twist.
The long head tendon runs inside the shoulder joint, which is why shoulder problems can cause pain in the front of the arm.

conditions.name: Biceps tendinitis
conditions.description: The tendon at the shoulder or elbow becomes inflamed, causing pain with lifting and overhead reaching.

conditions.name: Distal biceps tear
conditions.description: The tendon at the elbow can snap during a sudden heavy lift, making the muscle belly ball up toward the shoulder.

conditions.name: SLAP tear
conditions.description: The long head tendon attaches to a ring of cartilage in the shoulder socket that can tear, causing deep shoulder pain and clicking.

organs.name: Gluteus Maximus
organs.tagline: The biggest muscle in your body, built for climbing and standing tall.
organs.summary:
The gluteus maximus is the largest and heaviest muscle in your body. It forms the shape of your buttock, stretching from the back of the pelvis and the tailbone to the upper femur and a thick band of fascia that runs down the outside of the thigh. Its fibers run at a steep diagonal, which gives it enormous leverage.

It extends your hip, driving you up stairs, out of a chair, and up a hill. It also rotates your thigh outward and, through the iliotibial band, helps steady the knee. In walking it works less than you might think; in sprinting and climbing it works hard. Humans have a much larger gluteus maximus than our ape relatives, and its size is thought to reflect our upright posture and long-distance running.

functions.title: Extends the hip
functions.detail: It drives your leg backward to stand up, climb stairs, and sprint.

functions.title: Rotates the thigh outward
functions.detail: Its diagonal fibers turn the thigh and lower leg outward, a motion used when you cross your legs.

functions.title: Steadies the knee
functions.detail: Through the iliotibial band it helps control the knee during running and landing.

functions.title: Brakes a forward lean
functions.detail: When you bend to pick something up, it lengthens under load to keep your pelvis from tipping forward.

organs.location: It forms the bulk of the buttock, behind the pelvis and hip joint.
organs.size: It is the body's largest muscle, a slab several centimeters thick that spans the entire buttock.
facts: It is the largest muscle in the human body, but it does surprisingly little during a slow walk.
Our gluteus maximus is far larger than that of chimpanzees, and its size is linked to upright running.
The muscle attaches partly to the iliotibial band, a long strip of fascia that helps stabilize the knee.

conditions.name: Gluteal strain
conditions.description: A stretch or tear of the buttock muscle, usually from sprinting or sudden direction changes, causing pain with hip extension.

conditions.name: Gluteal tendinopathy
conditions.description: The tendons that attach the gluteal muscles to the femur become irritated, causing pain on the outside of the hip, especially when lying on that side.

conditions.name: Deep gluteal syndrome
conditions.description: The sciatic nerve can be compressed by muscles deep in the buttock, causing pain that travels down the leg.

organs.name: Quadriceps
organs.tagline: Four muscles on the front of your thigh that straighten your knee.
organs.summary:
The quadriceps femoris is not one muscle but four that share a single tendon. The rectus femoris runs down the middle of the front thigh, while the vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and vastus intermedius wrap around the femur beneath it. All four join the quadriceps tendon, which wraps the kneecap and continues as the patellar tendon to the shin.

Together they straighten your knee, the motion behind a kick, a step up, and a soft landing. The rectus femoris crosses both the hip and the knee, so it also helps lift your thigh. The kneecap acts like a pulley, increasing the tendon's leverage. This is the bulkiest muscle group in the body, and it is why the front of your thigh looks so different from the back.

functions.title: Straightens the knee
functions.detail: All four muscles pull through the kneecap to extend the knee, the motion of kicking a ball.

functions.title: Lifts the thigh
functions.detail: The rectus femoris also flexes the hip, helping you step up or kick.

functions.title: Absorbs landings
functions.detail: The group lengthens under load to slow your body as you land from a jump.

functions.title: Holds the kneecap in line
functions.detail: The vastus medialis helps keep the patella tracking toward the center of the knee.

organs.location: It fills the front of the thigh, from hip to kneecap.
organs.size: The four bellies together form the bulkiest muscle group in the body, wrapping the femur from hip to knee.
facts: The quadriceps is four muscles, but only the rectus femoris crosses the hip joint.
The kneecap is a sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps tendon, and it improves the tendon's leverage.
The vastus lateralis is the largest of the four and generates much of the force in a jump.

conditions.name: Quadriceps strain
conditions.description: A pulled thigh muscle, most often in the rectus femoris, causes pain and weakness when kicking or sprinting.

conditions.name: Patellofemoral pain
conditions.description: Pain around the kneecap is common when the quadriceps pull unevenly or the knee is loaded in a bent position.

conditions.name: Quadriceps tendon tear
conditions.description: A partial or complete tear above the kneecap makes it hard to straighten the knee and can cause the knee to give way.

organs.name: Hamstrings
organs.tagline: Three muscles behind the thigh that drive you forward and slow you down.
organs.summary:
The hamstrings are three muscles that run down the back of your thigh: the biceps femoris on the outside, and the semitendinosus and semimembranosus on the inside. All three reach the ischial tuberosity, the bony knob you sit on, and cross the knee to attach to the tibia and fibula. The biceps femoris has a second, short head that starts on the femur itself. Their tendons are the tough cords that frame the hollow behind your knee.

They bend the knee and extend the hip, so they power every stride and control the leg as it swings forward. During a sprint, they alternate between shortening hard and lengthening under load, which is why they are among the most commonly strained muscles in sport. Sit on your hands and lean forward; the pull you feel under your sitting bones is the hamstrings at work.

functions.title: Bends the knee
functions.detail: They flex the knee, drawing the heel toward the buttock as you prepare to step.

functions.title: Extends the hip
functions.detail: They drive the thigh backward in walking, running, and jumping, working with the glutes.

functions.title: Controls the leg's swing
functions.detail: They lengthen under load to slow the shin before the foot lands.

functions.title: Rotates the lower leg
functions.detail: When the knee is bent, they can turn the shin inward or outward.

organs.location: They run down the back of the thigh, from the sitting bone to the back of the knee.
organs.size: The three muscles together form a band about as wide as your hand, with the biceps femoris the thickest of the group.
facts: The hamstring tendons form the inner and outer walls of the hollow behind your knee.
All three bend the knee, but the short head of the biceps femoris starts on the femur, so it alone skips the hip.
In a sprint, they can be injured when they lengthen while contracting, which is why strains happen during acceleration.

conditions.name: Hamstring strain
conditions.description: A tear in one of the three muscles, usually during sprinting, causes sudden pain at the back of the thigh.

conditions.name: Proximal hamstring avulsion
conditions.description: The tendons can pull away from the sitting bone during a fall or a forceful stretch, causing deep buttock pain.

conditions.name: Hamstring tendinopathy
conditions.description: The tendon near the sitting bone becomes irritated, causing pain that worsens with sitting or running.

organs.name: Gastrocnemius
organs.tagline: The two-headed calf muscle that launches you onto your toes.
organs.summary:
The gastrocnemius is the muscle that gives your calf its bulge. It has two heads, one starting above each femoral condyle at the back of the knee, which merge into a broad belly and then into the Achilles tendon. That tendon is the thickest and strongest in the body, and it anchors the muscle to the heel bone.

When the gastrocnemius shortens, it points your toes and lifts your heel, the motion that carries you up onto tiptoe and pushes you forward in a run. Because it crosses the knee as well as the ankle, it also assists in bending the knee. A deeper muscle called the soleus lies beneath it, and together they form the triceps surae. Stand on the edge of a step and rise onto your toes, and you can feel this muscle do its work.

functions.title: Points the toes
functions.detail: Plantarflexion lifts your heel and pushes you forward, the motion of standing on tiptoe.

functions.title: Powers push-off
functions.detail: It stores and releases energy in the Achilles tendon with every step.

functions.title: Assists knee flexion
functions.detail: Because it crosses the knee as well as the ankle, it helps bend the joint when you lift your heel.

functions.title: Pumps blood upward
functions.detail: Calf contraction squeezes deep veins, helping blood return to the heart against gravity.

organs.location: It forms the bulging upper half of the calf, below the back of the knee.
organs.size: Its two bellies together are about as long as your hand in a relaxed leg and flatten into a tendon above the heel.
facts: Its name comes from the Greek words for belly and leg, because it makes the calf look like a belly.
It is built for quick, powerful pushes, while the soleus beneath it is built for endurance.
The Achilles tendon it feeds into is the strongest tendon in the body, able to withstand loads several times body weight.

conditions.name: Calf strain
conditions.description: A sudden stretch can tear fibers in the calf, often called tennis leg, causing sharp pain and a feeling of being kicked.

conditions.name: Achilles tendinopathy
conditions.description: The tendon below the calf becomes thickened and painful with repeated loading.

conditions.name: Achilles rupture
conditions.description: A complete tear can make an audible pop and leave you unable to push off on that leg.

organs.name: Diaphragm
organs.tagline: The dome beneath your lungs that pulls in every breath.
organs.summary:
The diaphragm is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle that separates your chest from your abdomen. It attaches around the lower ribs, the breastbone, and the lumbar spine, and its fibers converge on a central tendon that sits just below the heart. At rest it curves upward like an upside-down bowl.

When it contracts, the dome flattens downward, enlarging the chest cavity and drawing air into the lungs. It is the main muscle of quiet breathing, working about 20,000 times a day without your notice. It also helps raise pressure inside the abdomen for coughing and lifting, and it squeezes the esophagus to help keep stomach contents down. The phrenic nerve, which runs from the neck, is its main nerve supply, and damage to it can leave half the dome paralyzed.

functions.title: Draws air into the lungs
functions.detail: Contraction flattens the dome and lowers pressure in the chest, pulling air in.

functions.title: Drives quiet breathing
functions.detail: It does most of the work of breathing at rest, with help from the intercostal muscles.

functions.title: Raises abdominal pressure
functions.detail: It pushes down on the belly during coughing, lifting, and childbirth, adding force to the effort.

functions.title: Guards the esophagus
functions.detail: Its crura form a sling that helps prevent stomach contents from rising.

organs.location: It stretches across the bottom of the rib cage, separating the chest from the abdomen.
organs.size: It is a thin sheet only a few millimeters thick, spanning the width of the rib cage like a drumhead.
facts: It is the main muscle of breathing, but it also helps you cough, laugh, and push.
Its nerve arises in the neck, so irritation of the diaphragm can be felt as pain at the shoulder tip.
Hiccups are sudden involuntary contractions of the diaphragm followed by a quick closure of the vocal cords.

conditions.name: Hiatal hernia
conditions.description: Part of the stomach slides up through the opening in the diaphragm, which can cause heartburn and a feeling of fullness.

conditions.name: Diaphragm paralysis
conditions.description: Damage to the phrenic nerve or the muscle itself can weaken one side of the dome, causing shortness of breath when lying flat or exerting.

conditions.name: Hiccups
conditions.description: Brief involuntary contractions of the diaphragm, followed by a sudden closure of the vocal cords, produce the familiar sound.

lesson.title: The pull of a lifetime: a tour of your muscles
lesson.subtitle: From your shoulder cap to the muscle that breathes for you, follow the pull.

steps.title: Pull, never push
steps.body: Reach out and touch your opposite shoulder. Under your fingers is a rope of tissue that just changed length on command, pulling one bone toward another across a joint. That is the whole trick of skeletal muscle: it can only pull, never push, so it works in teams. One muscle bends a joint while its partner straightens it, and your brain chooses which to fire. You have more than 600 of these muscles, from the broad slab of your gluteus maximus to the tiny stapedius in your ear. We will start at the shoulder, work down through the trunk and hip, then double back to the muscle that breathes for you.

steps.title: The shoulder cap
steps.body: Lift your arm straight out to the side and hold it there. The rounded cap on top of your shoulder is the deltoid, and right now its middle fibers are working hard to keep your arm level. It has three parts, each pulling the upper arm from a different angle: front, side, and back. That arrangement lets one muscle swing your arm forward, out, and behind you. The deltoid also hugs the head of the arm bone, helping keep it seated in a socket shallower than a saucer. Next, follow the pull inward to the broad muscle crossing your chest.
steps.keyPoint: Three fiber angles let one shoulder muscle lift, reach, and pull back.

steps.title: The pushing fan
steps.body: Put your palms together and press. The wide fan across your chest tightens, pulling your arms toward the midline. That is the pectoralis major, and its fibers begin on the collarbone, breastbone, and upper ribs before converging into a single tendon on the arm. It adducts the arm, rotates it inward, and helps lift it forward. Because it crosses the front of the shoulder, it also adds stability. Boxers train it for punching, swimmers use it for the pull through water, and anyone pushing a heavy door uses it without thinking. Slide your hand down your side now, to the arm that does the pulling.
steps.keyPoint: The chest fan does the hugging motion and helps you breathe hard.

steps.title: The two-headed lifter
steps.body: Bend your elbow and watch the front of your arm rise. The biceps brachii has two heads at the shoulder that join into one belly, then one tendon that grips the radius. It bends the elbow, but its real talent is supination, turning your palm to face the ceiling. Try opening a tight jar with your palm down, then with your palm up; the second is easier because the biceps is doing more of the work. Its long tendon threads through the shoulder joint, which is why shoulder pain can show up as pain in the front of the arm. Now drop your hand to your belly and feel the corset underneath.
steps.keyPoint: The biceps is the forearm's strongest palm-up muscle, not just an elbow bender.

steps.title: Your inner corset
steps.body: Cough gently. The muscle that jumps under your hand is rectus abdominis, a long strap running from your pubic bone to your breastbone. It is one muscle, not six, crossed by bands of tendon that create the blocks people call a six-pack. It curls your trunk forward, braces your spine when you lift, and squeezes your belly to raise pressure when you cough or laugh. Two layers of fascia wrap it like a corset, and a pale seam called the linea alba divides left from right. Stand up and feel it engage, then follow the pull around to the back of your hip.
steps.keyPoint: A six-pack is one muscle marked by tendon bands, not six separate muscles.

steps.title: The climbing engine
steps.body: Stand up from a chair without using your hands. The muscle that launches you is the gluteus maximus, the largest and heaviest muscle in your body. It stretches from the back of your pelvis and tailbone to the femur and a long band of fascia down the outside of the thigh. It extends the hip, rotates the thigh outward, and steadies the knee through that band. Walking on flat ground barely asks it to work; climbing stairs, sprinting, and standing up demand almost everything it has. Our ancestors' upright stride helped shape its size. Now climb back up to your ribs, to the muscle that never stops.
steps.keyPoint: The biggest muscle in your body is built for climbing, not sitting.

steps.title: The muscle you forget
steps.body: Breathe in slowly and watch your belly rise. The muscle doing most of the work is the diaphragm, a dome of tissue under your lungs. When it contracts, it flattens and drops, enlarging the chest and pulling air in. It does this roughly 20,000 times a day, and you never feel it until something interrupts it, like a hiccup. It also presses down on your abdomen when you cough or lift, and its crura form a sling around the esophagus. Its nerve comes from your neck, which is why a diaphragm problem can be felt in the shoulder. One last stop: put the pieces together.
steps.keyPoint: The diaphragm is a muscle you drive thousands of times a day without noticing.

steps.title: Keep exploring
steps.body: Ten muscles, one idea: skeletal muscle pulls, and your skeleton redirects that pull into movement. The deltoid lifts, the pectoralis major adducts, the biceps bends and supinates, the rectus abdominis braces, the gluteus maximus drives, and the diaphragm breathes. Behind them sit four muscles we did not tour: the trapezius, which steadies the shoulder blade; the quadriceps and hamstrings, which drive and brake each stride; and the gastrocnemius, which launches every step. None of them works alone; each relies on partners, tendons, and nerves. Pick one muscle you felt today and explore its entry next. Then try the quiz and see which connections stuck.

quiz.question: Which part of the deltoid lifts your arm out to the side?
quiz.explanation: The middle, or lateral, fibers of the deltoid abduct the arm, lifting it away from the body. The front fibers flex the shoulder and the back fibers extend it.

quiz.question: Which muscle separates your chest cavity from your abdomen?
quiz.explanation: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscle that attaches to the lower ribs and spine and forms the floor of the chest, separating it from the abdominal cavity.

quiz.question: What is the biceps brachii especially good at doing?
quiz.explanation: The biceps bends the elbow, but its specialty is supination, turning the palm to face upward. It is the strongest supinator of the forearm.

quiz.question: Which quadriceps muscle also crosses the hip joint?
quiz.explanation: The rectus femoris begins on the pelvis and crosses both the hip and the knee, so it helps flex the hip as well as extend the knee. The vastus muscles cross only the knee.

quiz.question: What do the hamstrings do at the knee?
quiz.explanation: All three hamstrings cross the back of the knee and flex it, drawing the heel toward the buttock. They also extend the hip and can rotate the bent lower leg.

quiz.question: Why is the gluteus maximus so important for climbing stairs?
quiz.explanation: The gluteus maximus is a powerful hip extensor. Standing up, climbing, and sprinting all depend on it driving the thigh backward.

quiz.question: Why does a six-pack look like separate blocks?
options: The muscle is split into six separate muscles
Bands of tendon cross a single muscle
Fat pads sit between muscle strips
The linea alba divides it into six parts
quiz.explanation: Rectus abdominis is one long muscle. Three or four bands of tendon cross it, dividing the surface into blocks that become visible when body fat is low.

quiz.question: Which statement about the gastrocnemius is correct?
options: It has two heads and crosses both the knee and the ankle
It has one head and crosses only the ankle
It attaches to the heel through the patellar tendon
It is a smooth muscle found in the calf
quiz.explanation: The gastrocnemius has medial and lateral heads that begin above the knee and join the Achilles tendon. Because it crosses two joints, it helps bend the knee and point the ankle.
